**CHAPTER III**

**DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY**

This chapter presents the systematic process that will be used to develop and validate the proposed VIGILANT: A Virtual Inspection Gateway with Intelligent Logging and Access Network Traffic Control. Unlike traditional descriptive research, this study employs a developmental research design, focusing on the iterative cycle of analysis, design, development, and evaluation. The following sections detail the architectural framework of the project, the technical specifications involved, and the rigorous testing procedures used to ensure the final output meets the established standards of functionality, usability, and effectiveness.

RESEARCH DESIGN

This study follows a developmental research design, which is the methodology most appropriate for a capstone project whose primary goal is the creation of a functional technological system. The purpose is to design, build, and verify that VIGILANT works as intended, that it intercepts traffic transparently, that it categorizes content with meaningful accuracy, that it detects and throttles doomscrolling-associated request patterns, and that it does all of this without degrading network performance beyond acceptable limits. When the system meets those specifications, the research has achieved what it set out to do.

Developmental research is structured around a build-and-evaluate cycle. It refers to a systematic process of designing, developing, and evaluating products, processes, or systems to solve real-world problems. It focuses on generating practical solutions while simultaneously studying how those solutions are created and improved \[106\]. The study progresses through defined phases: the design of the system architecture, the implementation of its core components, and the technical testing of each component against predetermined performance benchmarks.

This approach aligns directly with the five specific objectives of the study. Objectives 1 through 3 govern the construction of the system's functional layers, from the transparent proxy interception mechanism and the NLP-based content categorization module to the behavioral throttling logic that responds to detected doomscrolling patterns. Objectives 4 and 5 govern its verification, measuring whether network throughput remains at or above 90% of the unfiltered baseline, whether latency stays within operationally acceptable bounds, and whether the administrative dashboard provides reliable real-time visibility into system activity.

The central research objective this design is built to answer is straightforward, and it is that VIGILANT performs its intended functions at a level of technical sufficiency suitable for household and small office deployment. Considering this, this research does not require a population of test subjects or a longitudinal observation period. It requires a working system and a rigorous testing protocol. Controlled network simulations, stress tests, and performance benchmarking under realistic load conditions, up to 30 concurrent connected devices in a controlled local environment, are sufficient to answer it.

The evaluation of VIGILANT focuses strictly on System Enforcement Accuracy and Technical Functional Validation. As a developmental research project, the success of the system is measured by its ability to execute programmed logic, specifically, its accuracy in identifying predefined traffic patterns (e.g., 'doomscrolling' signatures) and the successful application of bandwidth throttling or blocking rules. While the system will be designed to facilitate digital well-being, this study does not evaluate clinical psychological outcomes, such as changes in user addiction levels or long-term mental health improvements. Instead, the research verifies that the gateway correctly functions as a technical intervention tool according to the defined network parameters.

DESIGN STAGES OF THE PROCESS

The V-Model, also known as the Verification and Validation Model, is selected as the guiding Software Development Life Cycle framework for the development of VIGILANT because of its structured approach to quality assurance and its compatibility with the quantitative experimental nature of the study. Unlike iterative or agile models that prioritize flexibility and continuous delivery, the V-Model enforces a disciplined phase progression where each development stage is directly paired with a corresponding testing phase, ensuring that verification and validation activities are planned from the outset rather than addressed only after the system is built \[107\]. This characteristic is particularly well-suited to VIGILANT, as the system is composed of multiple interdependent components, a transparent proxy layer, an NLP-based content filtering engine, a behavioral throttling mechanism, and an administrative dashboard, each of which must be individually verified before system-level performance can be meaningfully evaluated. Because the study measures concrete technical outcomes such as network throughput efficiency and content filtering accuracy against predefined acceptance criteria, the V-Model's requirement that every development decision be traceable to a corresponding test outcome aligns directly with how the research will collect and validate its data. Furthermore, the structured phase progression of the V-Model prevents unresolved issues from carrying forward into later stages of development, which is critical in a controlled academic research setting where timeline constraints and reproducibility of results are essential considerations.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5. V-Model Software Development Life Cycle \[107\]

*Requirements Analysis*

During the Requirements Analysis phase, the research team will identify and document all functional and non-functional requirements of the VIGILANT system. This will include defining the need for transparent proxy interception via mitmproxy, NLP-based content filtering using spaCy's Named Entity Recognition, behavioral throttling for doomscrolling detection, and a Flask-based administrative dashboard. The team will also establish the measurable acceptance criteria that will later serve as the basis for system-level validation, such as the 90% throughput efficiency on the 8 GB RAM reference hardware configuration target and latency benchmarks. Stakeholder needs will be gathered and translated into clear system specifications to guide all subsequent development phases.

*System Design*

In the System Design phase, the overall architecture of the VIGILANT system will be defined. This will involve mapping out how the core components, the hostapd-based wireless access point, the mitmproxy SSL interception layer, the NLP filtering engine, the behavioral throttling module, and the web dashboard, will interact with one another within a unified gateway system. The team will also determine the hardware platform requirements and the deployment environment based on Ubuntu Server 24.04. Alongside the architectural design, system-level integration test plans will be prepared to ensure that the complete system can later be validated against the requirements established in the previous phase.

*Model Design*

The Model Design phase will focus on breaking down the overall system architecture into its major subsystems and defining the relationships and data flows between them. The team will detail how network traffic captured by the transparent proxy will be passed to the NLP engine for content categorization, how the categorization results will trigger throttling decisions, and how all activity will be logged and surfaced through the administrative dashboard. Interface designs between components will be established at this stage, and integration test cases will be drafted to verify that these subsystems work correctly together once development is complete.

*Coding* The Coding phase will involve the actual development of the VIGILANT system based on the designs produced in the preceding phases. The development team will write the source code for each module using Python 3.x, configure mitmproxy for transparent HTTPS interception, integrate the spaCy NLP pipeline for real-time content analysis, implement the behavioral throttling logic, and build the Flask-based web dashboard. The system will be developed in a localized Ubuntu Server 24.04 environment and will be structured so that each component aligns directly with its corresponding low-level design specification, enabling straightforward unit testing upon completion.

*Unit Testing*

In the Unit Testing phase, each individual module of the VIGILANT system will be tested in isolation to verify that it behaves according to its low-level design specification. The NLP content categorization module will be tested for classification accuracy using sample web content, the request-velocity monitor will be verified against predefined doomscrolling detection thresholds, the transparent proxy will be tested for correct traffic interception and SSL certificate handling, and the dashboard will be checked for accurate data rendering. Any defects identified during this phase will be resolved before the system proceeds to integration-level testing.

*Integration Testing*

The Integration Testing phase will verify that the individually tested modules of VIGILANT function correctly when combined into a unified system. Tests will confirm that traffic captured by the transparent proxy is successfully passed to the NLP engine, that classification results correctly trigger throttling responses, and that all relevant events are accurately logged and displayed on the administrative dashboard. This phase will address any interface inconsistencies or data flow errors that may not have been apparent during unit testing, ensuring that the subsystems operate cohesively before full system evaluation begins.

*System Testing*

During the System Testing phase, the fully assembled VIGILANT system will be evaluated as a complete, deployed gateway within a controlled test environment consisting of up to 30 concurrent connected devices. The team will conduct performance benchmarking by measuring key metrics including network throughput in megabits per second and latency in milliseconds, comparing results against the baseline to assess whether the system meets the 90% throughput efficiency on the 8 GB RAM reference hardware configuration target. The accuracy of contextual content filtering and doomscrolling detection will also be evaluated through simulated browsing scenarios, and the system's behavior under stress conditions will be observed to identify any performance bottlenecks.

*Acceptance Testing*

The Acceptance Testing phase will serve as the final validation of the VIGILANT system against the acceptance criteria established during the Requirements Analysis phase. The system will be assessed to confirm that all specific objectives have been met—including the correct operation of the transparent interception gateway, the reduction of over-blocking errors through NLP-based categorization, the functional accuracy of the doomscrolling detection and throttling mechanism, and the usability of the administrative dashboard. Results gathered during this phase will be used as the primary basis for evaluating the overall success of the system and will directly inform the conclusions drawn in the study.

DEVELOPMENT PROCESS

The development of VIGILANT was guided by a structured planning process rooted in the study's established research objectives and system requirements. Prior to writing any code, the researchers conducted a thorough review of the system's functional and non-functional requirements as defined in the Requirements Analysis phase of the V-Model SDLC. This ensured that every development decision remained aligned with the project's core goals: transparent traffic interception, context-aware NLP-based content filtering, behavioral doomscrolling detection, dynamic bandwidth throttling, and real-time administrative monitoring.

The conceptual framework served as the primary reference during planning, as it maps each system layer directly to a specific research objective. Layer 1, the Physical Access Layer, and Layer 2, the Traffic Interception Layer, correspond to Specific Objective 1, which requires the establishment of a transparent gateway with SSL/TLS interception and SNI fallback. Layer 3, the Semantic Analysis Layer, addresses Specific Objective 2 through NLP-based content categorization using spaCy Named Entity Recognition. Layer 4, the Behavioral Analysis Layer, and Layer 5, the Enforcement Layer, address Specific Objective 3 through request velocity monitoring and dynamic bandwidth throttling. Layer 6, the Monitoring and Management Layer, corresponds to Specific Objective 5, which calls for a Flask-based administrative dashboard. Finally, Layer 7, the Performance Evaluation Layer, supports Specific Objective 4 by establishing throughput and latency benchmarks.

User needs were identified through the research problem context defined in Chapter 1, particularly the need to address doomscrolling behavior and excessive screen time among students, households, and small office users in the Philippines without requiring manual device configuration or transmitting browsing data to third-party servers. These needs were translated into specific system behaviors during the planning stage, including the transparent access point setup using hostapd, the local-only edge processing architecture enforced through mitmproxy and spaCy running entirely on the host device, and the configurable filtering strictness controls accessible through the Flask dashboard. The implementation then proceeded module by module in accordance with the V-Model's coding phase, with each completed module submitted to unit testing before integration into the broader system.

Testing Process

The testing process describes the systematic execution of the VIGILANT system under controlled conditions with the intention of identifying errors, verifying correctness, and confirming that the system performs as intended across all defined requirements. Following the V-Model framework, three primary types of testing will be conducted in sequence: unit testing, system testing, and performance testing, each corresponding to a specific phase on the validation side of the V.

*Unit Testing*

Unit testing will be applied to individual components of VIGILANT to verify that each module functions correctly in isolation before being integrated with the rest of the system. The NLP classification module will be tested using a curated set of sample web page content spanning educational, social media, and news categories, with Named Entity Recognition output compared against manually labelled ground truth to confirm classification accuracy. The request velocity monitor will be tested by simulating rapid HTTP request sequences at and around the configured doomscrolling detection threshold to verify correct triggering behavior. The Flask API endpoints will be validated for correct HTTP response codes, proper JSON data formatting, and accurate persistence of filtering rule updates. The SQLite logging module will be verified for correct schema initialization, thread-safe write operations, and accurate data retrieval. Any failures identified during unit testing will be documented, resolved, and retested before the affected module proceeds to integration.

*System Testing*

System testing would evaluate the complete, integrated VIGILANT system against the functional requirements and acceptance criteria defined during the Requirements Analysis phase. Tests will be conducted in a controlled environment with up to 30 concurrent connected devices connected to the VIGILANT access point. Each of the five specific objectives will be tested individually: the system will be verified to intercept client traffic automatically without manual proxy configuration, the NLP filtering module will be evaluated for reduction of over-blocking errors relative to a baseline domain-only filter, doomscrolling detection triggered through simulated rapid scrolling sessions on targeted social media platforms, and the administrative dashboard verified to correctly display real-time activity and respond to filtering rule changes. System testing confirmed that all components functioned correctly together as a unified end-to-end pipeline.

*Performance Testing*

Performance testing assessed the ability of VIGILANT to sustain acceptable network performance under the additional computational load introduced by the proxy interception and NLP processing pipeline. Throughput will be measured in megabits per second using iPerf3 under both baseline conditions, with VIGILANT inactive, and active conditions, with the full interception and analysis pipeline running across multiple concurrent client sessions. Latency will be measured in milliseconds using ICMP ping tests to evaluate the round-trip delay introduced by the system. Throughput efficiency will be then computed as the ratio of active-to-baseline throughput expressed as a percentage, with the study targeting a minimum of 90% efficiency on the 8 GB RAM reference hardware configuration. Performance testing conducted across multiple trial runs to account for variability and ensure that results will be a statistical representation of the system’s actual operational behavior.

To specifically verify network reliability under peak demand, a structured stress-testing procedure will be executed as a sub-phase of performance testing. This procedure incrementally scales the number of simultaneously active client sessions from a single device to the full complement of 30 concurrent connected devices, adding five devices per load increment. At each increment, sustained iPerf3 TCP streams will be generated from every active client simultaneously for a minimum period of 120 seconds, after which throughput, latency, and packet loss figures are recorded. The VIGILANT host device’s CPU utilization, memory consumption, and mitmproxy queue depth will be sampled at five-second intervals throughout each load stage using the sar utility, enabling detection of resource exhaustion patterns before they manifest as measurable performance degradation. The stress-testing procedure is considered complete when either all 30 concurrent connected device load stages have been traversed without the system breaching the 90% throughput efficiency on the 8 GB RAM reference hardware configuration floor, or when a specific load threshold is identified at which performance degrades below the acceptance criterion. Any failure observed during stress testing initiates a Root Cause Analysis process, wherein system logs, sar resource profiles, and mitmproxy debug output are inspected in combination to isolate whether the degradation originates at the physical interface layer, within the iptables redirection chain, at the proxy processing pipeline, or within the NLP inference module. The identified failure point and its corresponding remediation are documented before the stress-test sequence is restarted from the lowest load increment to confirm that the corrective action restores compliance across all load stages.

Debugging Process

The debugging process is essential in software development and is crucial for ensuring that a system works correctly and efficiently. It involves identifying, analyzing, and fixing issues or defects in the codebase through a methodical process aimed at reducing the number of bugs present in the final system. For VIGILANT, debugging will be conducted throughout every phase of implementation and is not treated as a separate or terminal activity, but rather as an ongoing discipline integrated into the development workflow.

During the implementation of the mitmproxy interception addon, debugging focused on verifying the correct decryption of HTTPS traffic through the locally installed Root Certificate Authority, identifying and resolving SSL handshake failures caused by mobile applications implementing certificate pinning, and ensuring that the iptables redirection rules correctly routed all client TCP traffic to the proxy without affecting non-HTTP protocols unintentionally. Python's built-in logging module will be used throughout the addon script to produce timestamped debug output for each intercepted request, which allowed the researchers to trace the exact point of failure when exceptions occurred in the NLP pipeline or the velocity monitoring logic.

For the spaCy NLP module, debugging involved diagnosing cases where the Named Entity Recognition pipeline returned unexpected entity classifications on atypical web content such as single-page JavaScript applications that render content dynamically after the initial HTTP response. These cases will be identified through log inspection during unit testing and addressed by refining the content extraction logic within the mitmproxy addon to better handle response bodies with minimal or encoded text. The SQLite logging module will be debugged for thread-safety issues that emerged when multiple concurrent client sessions attempted simultaneous database writes, which will be resolved by implementing connection-per-thread access patterns. The Flask dashboard will be debugged for incorrect real-time data rendering caused by API endpoint caching behavior, which will be resolved by adjusting cache-control headers on relevant routes. All identified bugs and their resolutions will be documented to maintain a traceable record of system changes throughout the development lifecycle.

Validation Process

The validation process involves evaluating the software or system during or at the end of the development process to determine whether it satisfies the specified requirements. For VIGILANT, validation will be conducted at the conclusion of the development cycle and assessed how well the completed system fulfilled each of the five specific objectives established at the outset of the study. Validation will be carried out through a combination of functional validation, performance validation, and behavioral validation, each targeting a distinct area of the system.

*Functional Validation*

Functional validation confirmed that VIGILANT's core features operated correctly under realistic conditions. The transparent interception capability will be validated by connecting client devices with no manually configured proxy settings and confirming that all HTTP and HTTPS traffic is successfully intercepted and processed. The NLP content filtering module will be validated by measuring its Named Entity Recognition classification accuracy on a held-out test set of web page content, comparing the system's categorization decisions against manually verified labels to produce a precision and recall assessment. The doomscrolling detection mechanism will be validated by executing scripted browsing sessions that replicated rapid social media scrolling patterns and confirming that bandwidth throttling applied within the expected detection window. The administrative dashboard will be validated by verifying that all displayed traffic metrics and activity logs accurately reflect the underlying system state as confirmed through direct database inspection.

*Performance Validation*

Performance validation assessed whether VIGILANT met the quantitative network efficiency requirements defined in the study. Throughput and latency benchmarks collected during performance testing will be compared against the defined acceptance criterion of a minimum 90% throughput efficiency on the 8 GB RAM reference hardware configuration relative to the unfiltered baseline. Results will be evaluated across single-client and multi-client scenarios to determine whether performance degradation scaled acceptably with concurrent load. Latency measurements will be assessed to confirm that the processing overhead introduced by the proxy and NLP pipeline did not produce user-perceptible delays during normal browsing activity.

*Behavioral Validation*

Behavioral validation will evaluate the system's ability to correctly distinguish between productive and doomscrolling browsing patterns without generating excessive false positives that would throttle legitimate usage. Test sessions will be conducted across both targeted social media domains, where throttling is expected, and non-targeted educational and productivity domains, where throttling should not be applied. The proportion of correct throttling decisions relative to total detected velocity events will be recorded to assess the behavioral detection precision of the system. Collectively, the results of functional, performance, and behavioral validation will be used to determine whether VIGILANT fulfilled its role as a context-aware, privacy-preserving network gateway suitable for household, educational, and small office deployment.

PROGRAMMING PROCEDURE

This section outlines how the coding process is structured and provides insight into the development practices followed during the project. It highlights the specific tasks and decisions involved in transforming the system design and requirements into a functional, working solution.

The development of VIGILANT followed a structured and iterative approach, encompassing system architecture planning, requirements analysis, diagrammatic modeling, and implementation of its core components including the transparent proxy interception module, NLP-based content filtering engine, behavioral throttling mechanism, and the Flask-based administrative dashboard.

*System Architecture*

The system architecture of VIGILANT defines the high-level structure of the gateway system and illustrates how its major components interact to accomplish context-aware network traffic monitoring and control. The architecture is designed around an edge computing model, where all processing is performed locally on the host device, eliminating the need to transmit user data to external cloud servers, thereby preserving user privacy.

At the network layer, VIGILANT operates as a software-defined access point using hostapd, allowing client devices to connect to it wirelessly without requiring any manual proxy configuration. All outbound TCP and UDP traffic from connected clients is automatically intercepted and routed through the mitmproxy transparent proxy engine. Encrypted HTTPS traffic is decrypted using a locally installed Root Certificate Authority (Root CA), inspected, and then re-encrypted before being forwarded to its destination.

The intercepted HTTP/HTTPS content is passed to the NLP Processing Module, which uses the spaCy library (en\_core\_web\_sm model) to perform Named Entity Recognition (NER). This module analyzes the semantic content of web pages and categorizes them according to predefined content classifications. Simultaneously, the Request Velocity Monitor tracks the rate of network requests per client. When rapid scrolling patterns consistent with doomscrolling behavior are detected on targeted social media platforms, the system applies dynamic bandwidth throttling to the offending client session.

All events, filtering decisions, and network metrics are logged to a local SQLite database and surfaced in real time through the Flask-based Web Dashboard, which administrators can access from any browser on the local network. The figure below illustrates the overall system architecture of VIGILANT.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 6. System Architecture of VIGILANT

As shown in Figure 6, the VIGILANT system operates as the central intermediary between client devices and the external internet. Client devices connect to the VIGILANT access point and are assigned local IP addresses via the DHCP service. All traffic flows through the transparent proxy layer, which inspects HTTP traffic directly and decrypts HTTPS traffic through SSL interception. The NLP engine processes the content of intercepted web pages, while the request velocity monitor continuously evaluates behavioral patterns. Filtering decisions are enforced at the proxy layer, and all activity data is persisted to the local database and rendered on the administrative dashboard. This architecture ensures that all processing occurs at the network edge, maintaining low latency and full data privacy.

*Requirements Analysis*

Before defining the requirements of VIGILANT, a requirements analysis was first conducted on an existing system that operates within the same problem domain, a DNS-based content filtering system. Requirements analysis is the process of identifying, documenting, and validating the needs and conditions that a system must satisfy, taking into account the expectations of its intended users and the technical environment in which it will operate. By examining what a DNS-based filtering system is currently required to do, what performance standards it must meet, and what constraints prevent it from fully addressing the problem of excessive digital media consumption, the researchers were able to identify the specific gaps that VIGILANT must fill.

This analysis is organized into four categories: functional requirements, which define what the system must do; non-functional requirements, which define how well the system must perform; system constraints, which describe the technical limitations inherent to the existing approach; and identified gaps, which represent the unmet needs that directly shaped the design decisions behind VIGILANT. This structured analysis ensures that the development of VIGILANT is grounded not only in theoretical motivation but also in a traceable and evidence-based understanding of where existing solutions fall short.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 7. Requirements Analysis Diagram of VIGILANT

Figure 7 presents the requirements analysis conducted on an existing DNS-based content filtering system, which serves as the closest functional predecessor to VIGILANT in terms of problem domain and deployment context. The analysis identifies five functional requirements that such a system must fulfill: domain-level traffic interception, blacklist and whitelist management, DNS query logging, block page redirection, and upstream DNS forwarding to an external resolver. On the non-functional side, the system is expected to meet standards for performance, reliability, usability, scalability, and cross-device compatibility.

However, the analysis also reveals three critical system constraints that fundamentally limit the effectiveness of DNS-based filtering in modern network environments. First, filtering is confined strictly to the domain level, meaning the system cannot inspect the specific URL path or the actual content of a web page, making it incapable of distinguishing between legitimate and harmful material hosted on the same domain. Second, the system has no mechanism for decrypting HTTPS traffic, leaving the content of encrypted communications entirely unreadable. Third, the architecture is inherently bypassable, as users, particularly technically proficient ones, can circumvent all filtering rules by simply redirecting their DNS queries through a VPN or an alternate DNS provider. These constraints directly informed the design requirements of VIGILANT. The inability to perform contextual content analysis establishes the need for an NLP and Named Entity Recognition-based filtering engine; the absence of behavioral detection capabilities justifies the development of a request-velocity monitor with dynamic bandwidth throttling; and the bypassability of DNS-level filtering necessitates the adoption of transparent proxy interception, which operates at the network layer and captures traffic regardless of the DNS resolver in use.

*Use Case Diagram*

A Use Case Diagram shows the system's functionality from an external perspective, focusing on what the system will do based on user requirements. It identifies the actors that interact with the system and maps each actor to the specific functions, or use cases, available to them. For VIGILANT, the Use Case Diagram is developed to represent the complete set of interactions that external actors may initiate with or through the system.

Two primary actors were identified. The first is the Network Administrator, who interacts with VIGILANT directly through the Flask-based web dashboard using a browser on the local network. The administrator's use cases include monitoring real-time network traffic, reviewing the activity log, configuring content filtering rules, adjusting behavioral throttling thresholds, and managing connected client sessions. The second actor is the Client User, who interacts with VIGILANT indirectly by browsing the internet through a device connected to the VIGILANT access point. The client user's use cases include browsing the internet, receiving contextual content filtering based on NLP classification, and receiving bandwidth throttling when doomscrolling behavior is detected. A third implicit actor, the External Internet, represents the web servers and APIs that VIGILANT communicates with on behalf of connected clients. The Use Case Diagram is presented below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 8. Use Case Diagram of VIGILANT

As illustrated in Figure 8, the Use Case Diagram of VIGILANT clearly delineates the responsibilities and interaction boundaries of each actor. The Network Administrator is the only actor with direct access to the system's configuration and monitoring functions, maintaining administrative control over filtering behavior and system settings. The Client User, by contrast, interacts with the system entirely through normal browsing activity, with VIGILANT operating transparently in the background without requiring any configuration or awareness on the part of the client. This separation of actor roles reflects the system's design principle of providing intelligent, unobtrusive network management—where enforcement is automated and centrally administered rather than dependent on end-user compliance.

Context Diagram

A context diagram shows the system as a single process and illustrates how external actors—such as users, other systems, or external devices—interact with it. It provides the broadest possible view of the system's scope and its relationships with the outside world. For VIGILANT, the context diagram models the entire gateway as a single unified process called "VIGILANT System," and identifies all external entities that send inputs to or receive outputs from it.

The external entities identified in the VIGILANT context diagram are: (1) Client Devices, which generate internet traffic that flows into the system for inspection and receive filtered or throttled responses in return; (2) the Network Administrator, who sends configuration commands and filtering rule updates to the system and receives dashboard displays and activity reports; and (3) the External Internet, which receives forwarded and cleaned requests from VIGILANT and returns web content that is then inspected before being passed to the client. The context diagram is presented below.

Figure 9. Context Diagram of VIGILANT

As illustrated in Figure 9, the VIGILANT system sits at the center of its operational environment, receiving raw network requests from client devices and passing inspected, filtered traffic to the external internet. Responses from the internet are intercepted by VIGILANT before delivery to the client, allowing the system to enforce content policies in both directions of traffic flow. The Network Administrator interfaces with the system through the dashboard, which provides visibility into all traffic decisions and enables dynamic reconfiguration of filtering and throttling parameters. *Data Flow Diagram*

A Data Flow Diagram (DFD) is a graphical representation of the flow of data through a system, illustrating how input is transformed into output. It shows the processes that occur within the system, the data stores used, the external entities involved, and the data flows that connect these elements. The DFD for VIGILANT is modeled at Level 1 DFD , which decomposes the main process into its major sub-processes.

Data stores within the system include the Filtering Rules Database, which holds administrator-configured content policies; the Activity Log Database, which records all traffic events, NLP classifications, and throttling actions; and the Configuration Store, which maintains system settings and throttling parameters. The data flow diagram at Level 1 is presented below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 10. Data Flow Diagram (Level 1) of VIGILANT

As shown in Figure 10, the Level 1 DFD of VIGILANT illustrates the movement of data between each major sub-process. Raw client requests enter the Traffic Interception process and are decoded before being passed to the Content Analysis sub-process. Classified content data flows to both the Behavioral Monitoring sub-process and the Activity Log Database. The Behavioral Monitoring sub-process references the Filtering Rules Database and Configuration Store to determine whether to allow, block, or throttle the traffic. Enforcement decisions are applied by the Traffic Interception layer, and all outcomes are recorded in the Activity Log Database. The Dashboard Reporting sub-process continuously reads from the Activity Log Database and presents summarized and real-time data to the Network Administrator through the web interface. This DFD confirms that VIGILANT's data processing pipeline is fully contained within the local network environment, consistent with its edge computing design principles.

*Entity-Relationship Diagram*

The Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) illustrates the logical structure of the VIGILANT local SQLite database. The database is designed as an operational logging store rather than a relational transactional system, and as such, the four tables that comprise it are implemented as independent flat tables without enforced foreign key constraints. This design decision is consistent with SQLite's recommended usage for local, single-process logging applications and reflects the nature of VIGILANT's data, event records that are written continuously and independently by different system modules at runtime. The tables share common fields such as client\_ip and timestamp, which serve as natural join keys for analytical queries through the Flask dashboard, but no referential integrity is enforced between them at the database level.

The first table, traffic\_log, is the primary record of all intercepted network activity. It stores the client IP address, destination domain, HTTP method, protocol, timestamp, the NLP content category assigned by the spaCy engine, the filtering decision applied, and the HTTP response code. Every request that passes through the mitmproxy interception pipeline produces a corresponding entry in this table. The second table, throttle\_events, records each instance of bandwidth throttling triggered by the request velocity monitor. It stores the client IP, the time the throttle was triggered, the request count and detection window that triggered it, the target domain, the throttle level applied, and the time the throttle was released. The third table, filtering\_rules, holds the administrator-configured content filtering policies. Each record defines a target type such as a domain or NLP category, the target value, the action to apply, the strictness level, and whether the rule is currently active. The fourth table, config\_settings, stores system-wide configuration parameters as key-value pairs, including the velocity detection threshold, the throttle bandwidth cap, and the dashboard refresh interval. This table is read by the system at startup and may be updated by the administrator through the dashboard interface. The ERD is presented below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 11. Entity Relationship Diagram of VIGILANT

As shown in Figure 11, the four tables are presented as independent entities. The traffic\_log and throttle\_events tables share the client\_ip field, which allows throttling activity to be correlated with the specific browsing records that preceded it during dashboard queries. The filtering\_rules table is applied by the interception pipeline at runtime by loading active rules into memory at system startup rather than through a live database join on each request, keeping per-request processing overhead minimal. The config\_settings table likewise operates independently, with its values loaded into the system once at initialization. This flat, decoupled structure ensures that concurrent writes from multiple client sessions do not produce lock contention across tables, which is essential for maintaining the throughput efficiency targets defined in the study.

**TECHNICAL STANDARDS**

This section defines the required technical standards that govern the design, implementation, and evaluation of each layer in the VIGILANT system architecture. Adherence to these standards ensures inter-layer compatibility, reproducibility of test results, and provides a structured framework for Root Cause Analysis (RCA) when system failures or performance anomalies are encountered. The standards are organized in ascending order from the Physical Layer to the Application Layer, corresponding to the OSI reference model and mapped to VIGILANT’s internal layer designations.

*Required Standards per Layer*

Layer 1 – Physical Layer. The physical layer standard governs the hardware medium through which client devices connect to the VIGILANT gateway. The VIGILANT host device must be equipped with an IEEE 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) or higher-compliant wireless interface capable of sustaining a minimum aggregate throughput of 54 Mbps across all active client sessions under the 2.4 GHz band, or a minimum of 150 Mbps under the 5 GHz band. The Ethernet uplink between the VIGILANT host device and the home router must use a minimum Cat5e cable rated at 100BASE-TX, with a maximum segment length of 100 meters. Compliance with this layer is verified by confirming that baseline iPerf3 throughput measurements are not constrained by the physical medium prior to VIGILANT activation. RCA implication: if stress-test throughput degrades disproportionately at high client counts without elevated CPU or memory utilization, the root cause is attributable to physical-layer bandwidth saturation or driver-level Wi-Fi contention, and remediation involves frequency band adjustment or channel bonding configuration in hostapd.

Layer 2 – Data Link Layer. The data link layer standard governs the framing and MAC-level addressing within the local network segment. hostapd must be configured to operate in access point mode with WPA2-Personal (AES/CCMP) encryption as the minimum security standard, consistent with IEEE 802.11i. Ethernet frames between the VIGILANT host and the upstream router are processed at the Linux kernel’s bridging or routing layer and must conform to IEEE 802.3 framing standards. The dnsmasq DHCP service must assign private IPv4 addresses within a dedicated subnet (e.g., 192.168.100.0/24) that is topologically distinct from the upstream router’s DHCP pool. RCA implication: failures in HTTPS interception that present as SSL handshake errors at the proxy layer must first exclude Layer 2 causes, such as ARP resolution failures or IP address exhaustion in the DHCP pool, before attributing the failure to the mitmproxy certificate chain.

Layer 3 – Network Layer. The network layer standard governs IP routing and traffic redirection within the VIGILANT system. All client IPv4 traffic must be redirected through iptables PREROUTING rules in the NAT table, forwarding TCP traffic on ports 80 and 443 to mitmproxy’s listening port (default 8080) for transparent interception. IP forwarding must be enabled on the VIGILANT host via the kernel sysctl parameter net.ipv4.ip\_forward=1. The upstream default route must be reachable via the Ethernet interface, with DNS resolution delegated to dnsmasq. RCA implication: if client devices fail to receive filtered responses despite the proxy being active, a Layer 3 RCA requires inspecting iptables rule ordering with iptables -L -n -v, confirming that PREROUTING rules are not shadowed by ACCEPT rules in the FORWARD chain, and verifying that the default gateway is correctly propagated through dnsmasq to connected clients.

Layer 4 – Transport Layer. The transport layer standard governs the handling of TCP connection state within the mitmproxy transparent proxy. mitmproxy must maintain a concurrent connection pool sufficient to service all active client TCP sessions without queuing delays. The system is required to correctly perform the TLS termination and re-encryption cycle for all TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 connections, including proper handling of SNI (Server Name Indication) fields to construct per-host forged certificates. The iproute2 tc (traffic control) module must be capable of enforcing per-client bandwidth caps using the HTB (Hierarchical Token Bucket) queuing discipline on the access point network interface. RCA implication: if throttling fails to apply to a specific client session during stress testing, a Layer 4 RCA involves verifying that the tc qdisc and filter rules are correctly indexed to the offending client’s IP address, and that the HTB class hierarchy has not been inadvertently flushed by a concurrent iptables reload operation.

Layer 5 through 6 – Session and Presentation Layers. At the session layer, mitmproxy must correctly reconstruct multi-request HTTP/2 sessions by mapping individual streams to their parent session identifiers, preventing misrouting of interleaved responses to incorrect client connections during concurrent sessions. At the presentation layer, VIGILANT must correctly decode gzip, deflate, and br (Brotli) content-encoding formats before submitting response bodies to the spaCy NLP pipeline, ensuring that the NER module operates on plaintext rather than compressed byte sequences. RCA implication: classification anomalies on AJAX-heavy web applications are frequently attributable to a presentation-layer failure in content decoding, identifiable by inspecting the raw bytes passed to the spaCy pipeline against the Content-Encoding header of the intercepted response.

Layer 7 – Application Layer. The application layer standard governs the semantic processing and administrative interface components of VIGILANT. The spaCy NLP module must operate on the en\_core\_web\_sm model at minimum and must produce Named Entity Recognition classifications within an average inference latency of 50 milliseconds per response body under single-client conditions, degrading no more than linearly with additional concurrent sessions. The Flask administrative dashboard must serve all API endpoints with an HTTP 200 response code within 500 milliseconds under normal system load, and all dashboard data must reflect the current state of the SQLite activity log with a maximum staleness of one dashboard refresh interval. The SQLite logging module must execute write operations in a thread-safe manner using per-connection isolation, with no data integrity violations detectable after any completed stress-test run. RCA implication: dashboard data discrepancies reported against observed system behavior are traceable at the application layer by comparing Flask API response payloads directly against SQLite query results; persistent discrepancies indicate a caching anomaly at the Flask route level requiring cache-control header remediation.

Table I presents the software tools required for the development and operation of VIGILANT. Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS is selected as the operating system because it provides a stable, headless Linux environment that supports all required networking tools, including hostapd for access point configuration and iptables for traffic redirection, while consuming minimal system resources on edge hardware. Python 3.x serves as the primary development language due to its extensive ecosystem of networking and NLP libraries, and its direct compatibility with both mitmproxy's addon scripting interface and the Flask web framework.

Mitmproxy is chosen as the transparent proxy engine because it natively supports inline Python addons, enabling the interception pipeline, NLP processing, and throttling logic to be written as a single cohesive script rather than separate processes. spaCy with the en\_core\_web\_sm model provides lightweight Named Entity Recognition suited for real-time inference on resource-constrained hardware, striking a balance between classification accuracy and processing speed. hostapd and dnsmasq together enable the host device to function as a fully operational wireless access point with automatic IP assignment, eliminating the need for any manual network configuration on connected client devices. Flask is selected for the administrative dashboard because of its minimal overhead and straightforward routing model, which is sufficient for the dashboard's real-time log display and rule management requirements. SQLite 3 is chosen over a full database server because it operates as an embedded, serverless database within the same process, requiring no additional system services and storing all data locally without external dependencies. iPerf3 provides standardized and reproducible network throughput measurements, making it the appropriate instrument for the study's quantitative performance benchmarking objectives. Finally, the Virtual Machines will be used for a faster development environment, mimicking the client and server being developed.

INSTRUMENTATION

For a developmental study such as this, instrumentation refers to the tools and measurement instruments used to collect quantitative data during system evaluation. VIGILANT does not employ questionnaires or survey instruments, as the study's data collection is entirely technical in nature, focused on network performance metrics and system behavior observations.

Network throughput is measured using iPerf3, a standard open-source network performance tool that generates controlled TCP traffic streams between a client and server endpoint and reports the resulting bandwidth in megabits per second. Measurements will be taken under two conditions, with VIGILANT inactive as a baseline, and with VIGILANT fully active, across multiple trial runs to ensure consistent and representative results. Network latency is measured using ICMP ping, recording the round-trip time in milliseconds between a connected client device and an external reference host under both conditions.

The VIGILANT SQLite activity log served as the primary instrument for recording system behavior data, capturing every intercepted request, its NLP classification result, the filtering decision applied, and any throttling events triggered during the test sessions. NLP classification accuracy will be evaluated by comparing the system’s Named Entity Recognition output against a manually labelled reference set of web page content, using precision and recall as the primary accuracy metrics. Throttling precision will be assessed by reviewing the activity log for the ratio of correct throttling events on targeted social media domains relative to total velocity-triggered events across all test sessions.

*Quantitative Metrics: Threshold Values and Averages for Doomscrolling Detection and Throttling*

Request Velocity Thresholds. The Request Velocity Threshold (RVT) is the rate parameter monitored to detect doomscrolling behavior, formally defined as the count of HTTP GET requests from a single client IP address to a targeted social media domain within a 10-second sliding window. The baseline RVT for non-pathological browsing behavior is 4–8 requests per 10-second window. The doomscrolling detection threshold is set to 30 requests per 10-second window, representing approximately 4 times the mean of normal browsing activity. This threshold was derived from empirical analysis of infinite-scroll feed mechanisms, which typically issue 3–6 network requests per visible content segment. Throttling is triggered when RVT ≥ 30, applying a 128 Kbps bandwidth cap for 60 seconds. The acceptance criterion for Objective 3 is that throttling initiates within 10 seconds of threshold crossing in ≥95% of test trials, with <5% false positive rate on non-targeted domains.

Interception Rate Measurement. The Interception Rate, denoted as I(t), represents the number of unique HTTP/HTTPS requests successfully captured and processed by the mitmproxy transparent proxy layer per unit time (measured in requests per second). This metric validates Objective 1 (transparent traffic interception). The target Interception Rate must sustain a minimum of 500 requests per second under the 30-device concurrent load condition, with zero loss of requests at the transport layer. Request loss is detected by comparing the total request count recorded in the SQLite activity\_log against the total requests issued by iPerf3 client instances, with an acceptance criterion of less than 0.1% packet loss across all test trials.

Specific Objective 3 requires the system to detect doomscrolling behavior through the monitoring of request velocity and to respond by dynamically throttling the bandwidth available to the offending client session. The quantitative operationalization of this objective depends on two precisely defined threshold parameters stored in the config\_settings table and evaluated continuously by the Request Velocity Monitor module. The primary detection threshold is defined as a request velocity of 30 HTTP GET requests per 10-second sliding window, originating from a single client IP address against a targeted social media domain (e.g., twitter.com, facebook.com, instagram.com, tiktok.com). This threshold value was derived from empirical observation of typical doomscrolling interaction patterns, wherein infinite-scroll feed mechanisms issue between 3 and 6 network requests per visible content segment loaded, implying that a scrolling rate generating more than five content loads within 10 seconds constitutes a statistically anomalous and sustained consumption pattern. The average non-doomscrolling browsing baseline, established through instrumented reference sessions, generates a request velocity of between 4 and 8 HTTP GET requests per 10-second window on the same domain categories, yielding a detection threshold that is approximately 4 times the observed mean of non-pathological browsing behavior.

Request velocity is calculated as a time-windowed rate parameter by the velocity monitoring logic within the mitmproxy addon script. Formally, for a given client IP address c and a target domain d, the request velocity V(c, d, t) at evaluation time t is defined as the count of HTTP GET requests issued by c to any URL within d during the half-open interval \[t - W, t), where W is the configurable detection window width (default W = 10 seconds). The velocity monitor maintains a per-client, per-domain deque data structure that stores the Unix timestamp of each intercepted GET request. On each new intercepted request, timestamps older than t - W are purged from the deque, and the resulting length of the deque is taken as V(c, d, t). This sliding-window approach ensures that the velocity metric responds immediately to bursts without requiring a fixed epoch boundary, and that it naturally decays as request activity subsides. The throttling response is triggered when V(c, d, t) exceeds the configured threshold T (default T = 30), at which point the iproute2 tc module applies a bandwidth cap of 128 Kbps to all traffic from client c for a configurable throttle duration (default 60 seconds). The throttle is released automatically after the duration expires, and V is monitored continuously to detect recurrence. The acceptance criterion for Objective 3 is that the throttling response is initiated within one detection window (10 seconds) of the threshold being crossed in no fewer than 95% of test trials, with a false positive rate below 5% on non-targeted domains as measured across all behavioral validation sessions.

PREPARATION AND EVALUATION

Prior to conducting system evaluation, the test environment will be prepared to ensure controlled and reproducible conditions. The VIGILANT host device will be configured with Ubuntu Server 24.04, with all required software dependencies installed and verified. The hostapd access point is configured to broadcast a dedicated test network, and dnsmasq is set up to provide DHCP address assignment to connecting client devices. The mitmproxy Root Certificate Authority will be generated locally and installed on all test client devices to enable HTTPS interception. iptables rules will be applied to redirect all outbound TCP traffic from client devices through the mitmproxy transparent proxy. The SQLite database is initialized with a clean schema, and the Flask dashboard will be verified to be accessible from all test client devices on the local network prior to each evaluation session.

Evaluation will be conducted in two stages. The first stage measured baseline network performance with VIGILANT inactive, establishing reference throughput and latency values against which the system's overhead could be quantified. The second stage activated the full VIGILANT pipeline and repeated the same measurements under identical network conditions with up to 30 concurrent connected devices. Throughput efficiency is then computed by dividing the active-condition throughput by the baseline throughput and expressing the result as a percentage. Functional evaluation covered each specific objective in sequence, with pass or fail outcomes recorded against the acceptance criteria defined during the Requirements Analysis phase. All evaluation results will be logged directly from the system's own activity database and iPerf3 output reports, ensuring that the data is objective and traceable to specific test runs.

*Participants of the Study*

Given the technical and developmental nature of this study, VIGILANT does not involve human participants in the traditional research sense. No surveys, interviews, or behavioral observations of individuals were conducted. The study focuses entirely on the design, implementation, and technical performance evaluation of the proposed gateway system.

Figure 11. VIGILANT Inline Security Gateway Deployment and High-Density Network Simulation Topology

Figure 11 illustrates the physical deployment topology, interface assignments, and infrastructure scaling architecture designed to validate the V.I.G.I.L.A.N.T. gateway framework under stress conditions. The layout maps a deterministic hierarchical tree progressing down from the public internet down to the localized endpoint subnet. The perimeter border is established via a generic Wide Area Network (WAN) Cloud, which bridges directly into a Cisco 2911 Integrated Services Router (ISR) acting as the Internet Service Provider (ISP) demarcation edge node.

Positioned strictly inline between the external ISP edge and the local intranet sits the V.I.G.I.L.A.N.T. Gateway Appliance, modeled as an Ubuntu Server platform explicitly scoped to an 8GB System RAM execution baseline. The diagram highlights dual physical Network Interface Cards (NICs) configured to enforce rigid traffic routing parameters. The inbound interface acts as the dedicated ingestion sink hooked directly into the upstream ISP router’s gateway port. The outbound interface runs an internal DHCP server daemon (dnsmasq) and maps the downstream local private network framework (192.168.1.0/24), routing all untrusted internal client data packets natively through the proxy layer before they can touch the external interface.

Distributing the network footprint further down, the outbound gateway pipeline trunks directly into a Cisco Catalyst 2960 24-Port Layer 2 Switch. This switch acts as the physical aggregation layer for high-density clients, multiplexing traffic from an enterprise-grade 802.11ax Wi-Fi 6 Wireless Access Point (AP) alongside physical wired terminal stations. To explicitly fulfill the panel's mandate of measuring real-world system resilience against severe multi-user load conditions, the subnet layout features distinct physical endpoint icons—including desktop administrative platforms, mobile research workstations, and active multi-media smartphones—coexisting alongside a dedicated Network Load Simulation Subnet Cluster. This simulation node dynamically populates the local switching matrix with 27 simulated endpoint terminals, building a verified testing scale of 30 concurrent active connections executing deep packet inspection and natural language parsing simultaneously.

*System Flowchart*![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 12. V.I.G.I.L.A.N.T. Sequential Network Packet Processing and Enforcement Flowchart

Figure 12 details the operational execution pipeline and runtime decision-making logic of the V.I.G.I.L.A.N.T. gateway appliance as it captures and evaluates transit network packets. The system loop begins with the continuous ingestion of inbound IP packets arriving from local client nodes. At the network perimeter, the packet header data is evaluated by the Linux kernel’s packet-filtering architecture via a customized Netfilter/iptables hook. If the packet protocol is identified as standard background noise, non-HTTP/HTTPS traffic, or originates from a bypassed domain, it exits the interception chain immediately through the Standard Forwarding Pipeline, proceeding directly to the Wide Area Network (WAN) to ensure network transparency for non-targeted traffic.

For standard port 80 (HTTP) and port 443 (HTTPS) traffic streams, an active PREROUTING rule forces a kernel-level redirection to a locally bound mitmproxy daemon listening internally on port 8080. Cryptographic session termination is achieved as the proxy intercepts the TLS handshake, dynamically mints a site-specific X.509 certificate anchored to the gateway’s pre-trusted local Root CA, and establishes an isolated, mirrored session with the destination web server. Once the payload is securely decrypted at the application layer, the architecture splits packet evaluation into two parallel, non-blocking asynchronous processing threads: The volumetric thread, it tracks and aggregates individual connection metadata to calculate real-time user request frequencies (Request Velocity) within a designated sliding time window; The semantic thread, it feeds extracted plain-text application layer elements into the localized spaCy NLP classification pipeline to assign weighted probability scores across four predetermined restrictive behavioral categories.

The structural output flags from both parallel modules are piped into a central conditional logic engine. If the request volume falls safely below the designated behavioral caps or fails to score heavily within targeted distraction categories, the engine clears the packet for standard routing, maintaining a target transmission threshold efficiency of 90% relative to the unfiltered baseline. Conversely, if the request velocity matches a severe "doomscrolling" fingerprinted signature and correlates with high-density target content keywords, the system switches to the Traffic Enforcement Layer. Here, an adaptive token-bucket or delayed-queue algorithm chokes downstream throughput bandwidth, logs the complete telemetry incident report (timestamp, client IP, velocity metric, and structural category classifications) into the local SQLite activity\_log database, and forwards the heavily managed packet stream to the WAN to systematically break high-frequency cognitive feedback loops.

*Setup Agreement Schematic*

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 13. VIGILANT System Configuration and Consent Workflow Schematic.

Figure 13 illustrates the prerequisite initialization sequence, technical layer integration, and user informed-consent checkpoints required before a client node can actively traverse the VIGILANT gateway framework. Structurally mapped as a three-lane enterprise workflow, the schematic delineates clear operational boundaries between the Network Administrator, the VIGILANT Host Device (Ubuntu Server Baseline), and the Client Device.

The pipeline begins in the Administrator lane with the local generation of a cryptographic Root Certificate Authority (CA), isolating the private execution key within the host storage to protect the cryptographic boundaries of the gateway. The process then transitions directly to the Client Device lane, requiring a manual, explicit import of the root certificate into the local trust store. This milestone acts as the system's objective checkpoint for informed user consent; any client device lacking this certificate configuration will automatically fail the mandatory SSL/TLS handshake termination, decoupling unconsented endpoints from application-layer analysis.

Once the certificate is trusted, the client associates with the VIGILANT Wi-Fi Access Point, triggering the automated Host lane sequence. A local dnsmasq daemon handles DHCP address assignment verification to lock the client's internal IP footprint. Following lease confirmation, kernel-level iptables rules capture outbound TCP flows over ports 80 and 443, redirecting them to the local mitmproxy listener interface, verified dynamically via internal conntrack state tables. Simultaneously, a parallel background process executes an NLP pipeline warmup, pre-loading the heavy semantic weights of the spaCy intelligence model to optimize inference velocity before active payload ingestion.

The final integration stage involves an end-to-end accessibility check where the Administrator verifies Flask web-dashboard reachability from the client browser, followed by resetting the SQLite activity log database to ensure a clean transaction baseline. The system achieves complete operational status once the client acknowledges a localized web notice confirming active, transparent network management under an optimized 90% throughput efficiency profile across the 30 concurrent connected device target load. Conditional PASS/FAIL logic gates integrated across each technical milestone enforce structural error recovery, requiring immediate rollback or routing table flushes if an internal subsystem fails verification.

ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS

The development of VIGILANT will be conducted with careful attention to the ethical responsibilities associated with a system that operates at the network level and intercepts user traffic. The following considerations guided the design and implementation of the system throughout the study.

**Data Privacy**. All traffic inspection and NLP processing occur entirely on the VIGILANT host device and will be never transmitted to external servers. The activity log retains only the client IP address and behavioral metadata necessary for system operation, and no personally identifiable browsing content will be stored beyond what is required for real-time classification. This local-only architecture ensures compliance with the spirit of the Data Privacy Act of 2012 of the Philippines.

**Informed Consent.** VIGILANT is intended for deployment in environments where the network administrator holds authority over the network, such as households, classrooms, and small offices. The Root Certificate Authority required for HTTPS interception must be manually installed on each client device, which serves as an explicit point of disclosure. Individuals who install the certificate are knowingly participating in the monitored network, and the system does not intercept encrypted traffic on devices that have not accepted the certificate.

**Security.** The Root CA private key is generated locally and never shared externally. The administrative dashboard is accessible only within the local network and is not exposed to the public internet. All system data will be stored on the host device's local filesystem. The researchers note that VIGILANT is a research prototype and recommend that future production deployments include additional hardening measures such as dashboard authentication and encrypted log storage.

**Intellectual Property.** All software components used in VIGILANT are open-source tools licensed for research and educational use, including mitmproxy, spaCy, Flask, and Python. The system is an original work of the researchers, and all referenced works are cited in accordance with IEEE standards.

**Algorithmic Fairness and Responsible Use.** The researchers acknowledge that the spaCy en\_core\_web\_sm model is trained primarily on English-language text and may perform less accurately on Filipino or code-switched content. Filtering rules are administrator-configurable to allow manual correction of misclassifications. The system will be developed to promote healthier digital habits and is not intended for covert surveillance or unauthorized monitoring of individuals.
